Saint Augustine Confusion. Two major figures named Saint Augustine lived over two centuries apart, and they are frequently conflated despite very different roles and legacies. Augustine of Hippo lived from 354 to 430 and was a North African theologian whose writings shaped Christian doctrine. Augustine of Canterbury lived from around 540 to 604 and was a missionary who brought Christianity to Anglo-Saxon England. Confusion is especially common because both are venerated as saints and both profoundly influenced Christianity, yet in entirely different contexts.

Augustine of Hippo was born in Roman North Africa, converted to Christianity as an adult, became a bishop, and wrote Confessions and City of God—foundational texts of Christian theology. Augustine of Canterbury was an Italian-born Benedictine monk sent by Pope Gregory I to evangelize the Anglo-Saxons. He established the Archbishop of Canterbury and is considered the founder of the English church.

Augustine of Hippo lived in late antiquity and the early medieval period. Augustine of Canterbury lived in the early medieval period, separated from the first by over a century. Augustine of Hippo's influence was primarily theological and philosophical, shaping doctrines of original sin, grace, and the nature of the church. Augustine of Canterbury's influence was primarily ecclesiastical and missionary.

Augustine of Hippo is the more famous and widely cited figure in academic and theological contexts. Augustine of Canterbury is primarily significant in British and English church history. Both are commemorated as saints. Augustine of Hippo's feast day is August twenty-eighth, while Augustine of Canterbury's is May twenty-sixth.
